title: Zener Regulators
description: Use a zener diode in reverse breakdown with a series resistor to hold a load voltage constant.

study.title: The zener diode
study.body: A zener diode is made to operate in **reverse breakdown**. In breakdown the voltage from cathode to anode stays close to the zener voltage $V_Z$ over a wide range of current, so it acts as a voltage reference. With the usual diode references $v_D = -V_Z$ and $i_D < 0$; it is easier to work with the positive reverse current $I_Z = -i_D$, flowing into the cathode.

study.title: The shunt regulator
study.body: A series resistor $R$ drops the difference between the supply and $V_Z$, and the zener in parallel with the load holds $v_o \approx V_Z$. While the zener is in breakdown, the current through $R$ is set by the supply alone, not by the load.

study.title: Sharing the current
study.body: KCL at the output node: the resistor current splits into the zener current and the load current $I_L = V_Z/R_L$. The zener takes whatever the load does not. With no load, all of $I_R$ flows through the zener.

study.title: Staying in breakdown
study.body:
The zener only regulates if $I_Z \ge I_{Z,min}$. This limits the load current and the load resistance:
$$I_{L,max} = \frac{V_{s,min} - V_Z}{R} - I_{Z,min}, \quad R_{L,min} = \frac{V_Z}{I_{L,max}}$$
If the load is too heavy, the zener turns off and the output is just a divider: $v_o = V_s\frac{R_L}{R + R_L} < V_Z$. Quick test: the zener is in breakdown only if this divider voltage exceeds $V_Z$.

study.title: Power ratings
study.body: The zener dissipates $P_Z = V_Z I_Z$. The worst case is **maximum supply and no load**, because then all of $I_R$ flows through the zener. The resistor dissipates $P_R = (V_s - V_Z)^2/R$, also largest at maximum supply.

study.title: Design and non-ideal zeners
study.body:
Design: choose $V_Z$ = desired output, then pick $R$ small enough to deliver $I_{L,max} + I_{Z,min}$ at the lowest supply, then check the power at the highest supply.
$$R \le \frac{V_{s,min} - V_Z}{I_{L,max} + I_{Z,min}}$$
A real zener in breakdown has a small resistance $R_Z$ (piecewise-linear model: source $V_Z$ in series with $R_Z$). Without load, a supply change $\Delta V_s$ then gives $\Delta v_o = \Delta V_s\frac{R_Z}{R + R_Z}$.

steps.title: Breakdown on purpose
steps.body: A zener diode is built to work in **reverse breakdown**. Once the reverse voltage reaches $V_Z$, current flows from cathode to anode while the voltage stays almost constant. That makes it a simple voltage reference: think of it as a $V_Z$ battery that only works in one direction.

steps.prompt: In a regulator fed from a positive supply, how is the zener connected?
options: Cathode to the positive output node, anode to ground
Anode to the positive output node, cathode to ground
In series between the resistor and the load
steps.explanation: The zener must be **reverse** biased to reach breakdown, so its cathode goes to the positive node. Connected the other way it would be forward biased and clamp the output at about 0.7 V.

steps.prompt: A zener diode in breakdown keeps its voltage close to $V_Z$ even when its current changes a lot.
steps.explanation: In breakdown the characteristic is nearly vertical: large changes in current give only tiny changes in voltage. That is exactly why it can regulate a voltage.

steps.title: The regulator circuit
steps.body: The resistor $R$ absorbs the difference between the (varying) supply and $V_Z$; the zener holds the output at $V_Z$. The current through $R$ is $I_R = (V_s - V_Z)/R$.

steps.prompt: The zener is in breakdown. Find the current $I_R$ through the series resistor.
steps.explanation:
The output node sits at $V_Z$, so $R$ has $V_s - V_Z$ across it:
$I_R = \frac{ {{Vs}} - {{VZ}} }{ {{R}} }$ = {{(Vs-VZ)/R|A}}.
$R_L$ doesn't enter: the load only decides how $I_R$ is split.

steps.prompt: While the zener stays in breakdown, connecting a heavier load (smaller $R_L$) increases the current drawn from the supply.
steps.explanation: The supply current is $I_R = (V_s - V_Z)/R$, which does not depend on $R_L$. A heavier load just takes a bigger share of $I_R$, and the zener current drops by the same amount.

steps.title: Who gets the current?
steps.body: KCL at the output node: $I_R = I_Z + I_L$, with $I_L = V_Z/R_L$. The zener takes the rest.

steps.prompt: With $V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}} and $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}, find the zener current $I_Z$ (the zener is in breakdown).
The load of a working zener regulator is disconnected. What happens?
options: $I_Z$ rises to $I_R = (V_s - V_Z)/R$ and $v_o$ stays $\approx V_Z$
steps.explanation: With $I_L = 0$, KCL gives $I_Z = I_R$, its maximum value. The output stays at $V_Z$ (the zener is still in breakdown). This is also the case of maximum zener power dissipation.

steps.prompt: The zener stays in breakdown while $R_L$ is changed. Tap every element whose current does **not** change.
steps.explanation:
In breakdown the zener holds the output at $V_Z$. The voltage across $R$ is then fixed, $V_s - V_Z$, so its current
$$i_R = \frac{V_s - V_Z}{R}$$
does not depend on the load. That current is shared: $i_R = i_Z + i_L$. When $R_L$ changes, $i_L = V_Z/R_L$ changes and the zener current changes by the opposite amount.

steps.prompt: The load draws a constant $I_L$ = {{IL|A}}. Find the zener current $I_Z$.
A regulator has $V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}} and $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}. How much power does the zener dissipate?
A regulator has $V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}}. The zener needs at least $I_{Z,min}$ = {{Izm|A}} to stay in breakdown. What is the largest load current it can supply?
steps.explanation:
$I_R = ({{Vs}} - {{VZ}})/{{R}}$ = {{IR|A}}, fixed by the supply. The zener must keep at least $I_{Z,min}$, so
$I_{L,max} = I_R - I_{Z,min}$ = {{IR|A}} − {{Izm|A}} = {{IR-Izm|A}}.

steps.prompt: Same kind of regulator: $V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}}, $I_{Z,min}$ = {{Izm|A}}. What is the smallest load resistance $R_L$ for which the output stays regulated?
steps.explanation:
$I_{L,max} = \frac{V_s - V_Z}{R} - I_{Z,min}$ = {{ILm|A}}.
The load voltage is $V_Z$, so $R_{L,min} = V_Z/I_{L,max} = {{VZ}}/{{ILm}}$ = {{VZ/ILm|Ω}}. A smaller $R_L$ would draw more current and starve the zener.

steps.prompt: A regulator with $V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}} may be operated without a load. What is the worst-case zener power?
steps.explanation:
Without a load, all of $I_R$ flows in the zener: $I_Z = ({{Vs}} - {{VZ}})/{{R}}$ = {{(Vs-VZ)/R|A}}.
$P_Z = V_Z I_Z$ = {{VZ*(Vs-VZ)/R|W}}. The zener's power rating must exceed this.

steps.prompt: A regulator has $V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, a {{VZ|V}} zener and a heavy load $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}. What is the output voltage $v_o$ across $R_L$?
steps.explanation:
Check whether the zener can be in breakdown: with the zener removed, $v_o = V_s\frac{R_L}{R + R_L} = {{Vs}}\times\frac{ {{RL}} }{ {{R}} + {{RL}} }$ = {{Vs*RL/(R+RL)|V}}.
This is **less** than $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}}, so the zener never reaches breakdown and carries no current. The output is just the divider voltage: the load is too heavy for this regulator.

steps.prompt: The zener dissipates the most power when the load is disconnected and the supply voltage is at its maximum.
steps.explanation: $P_Z = V_Z I_Z$ with $I_Z = (V_s - V_Z)/R - I_L$. This is largest for the largest $V_s$ and $I_L = 0$. Size the zener's power rating for this case.

steps.prompt: Design a regulator for a {{VZ|V}} output. The supply can drop to {{Vmin|V}}, the load draws up to {{ILm|A}}, and the zener needs at least {{Izm|A}}. What is the largest allowed series resistance $R$?
steps.explanation:
The hardest case is the lowest supply with the largest load. Then $R$ must still deliver $I_{L,max} + I_{Z,min}$:
$R \le \frac{V_{s,min} - V_Z}{I_{L,max} + I_{Z,min}} = \frac{ {{Vmin}} - {{VZ}} }{ {{ILm}} + {{Izm}} }$ = {{(Vmin-VZ)/(ILm+Izm)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: The regulator uses $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and a {{VZ|V}} zener. The supply can rise to {{Vmax|V}} and the load may be disconnected. What is the worst-case zener power?
steps.explanation:
Worst case: maximum supply, no load, so $I_Z = I_R = ({{Vmax}} - {{VZ}})/{{R}}$ = {{(Vmax-VZ)/R|A}}.
$P_{Z,max} = V_Z I_Z$ = {{VZ*(Vmax-VZ)/R|W}}.

steps.prompt: For the same kind of regulator ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}}, supply up to {{Vmax|V}}), what power rating does the series resistor need at least?
steps.explanation:
The resistor always has $V_s - V_Z$ across it, whatever the load. Worst case at maximum supply:
$P_R = \frac{(V_{s,max} - V_Z)^2}{R} = \frac{({{Vmax}} - {{VZ}})^2}{ {{R}} }$ = {{(Vmax-VZ)^2/R|W}}.

steps.prompt: A regulator has $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}}, load $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} and $I_{Z,min}$ = {{Izm|A}}. What is the lowest supply voltage for which the output is still regulated?
steps.explanation:
At the limit the zener carries just $I_{Z,min}$, and the load takes $V_Z/R_L$ = {{VZ/RL|A}}. So $I_R = I_{Z,min} + I_L$ = {{Izm+VZ/RL|A}} and
$V_{s,min} = V_Z + R\,I_R = {{VZ}} + {{R}}\times{{Izm+VZ/RL}}$ = {{Vmin|V}}.

steps.prompt: A real zener in breakdown is modeled as a source $V_Z$ in series with $R_Z$ = {{RZ|Ω}}. With series resistor $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and no load, the supply rises by {{dVs|V}}. By how much does the output voltage rise?
steps.explanation:
For changes, the $V_Z$ source is constant, so $R$ and $R_Z$ form a voltage divider for $\Delta V_s$:
$\Delta v_o = \Delta V_s\frac{R_Z}{R + R_Z} = {{dVs}}\times\frac{ {{RZ}} }{ {{R}} + {{RZ}} }$ = {{dVs*RZ/(R+RZ)|V}}.
A small $R_Z$ and a large $R$ give good line regulation.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of designing a zener regulator in order
items: Choose a zener with $V_Z$ equal to the desired output
Compute the largest $R$ that gives $I_Z \ge I_{Z,min}$ at minimum supply and maximum load
Pick a standard resistor value at or below that limit
Compute the worst-case powers at maximum supply with no load
Choose zener and resistor power ratings above those values
steps.explanation: The minimum-supply/maximum-load case sets the upper limit on $R$. The resulting $R$ then fixes the worst-case dissipation (maximum supply, no load), which sets the power ratings.

steps.prompt: The supply of a regulator varies from {{Vmin|V}} to {{Vmax|V}}; $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, $V_Z$ = {{VZ|V}}, $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}. Find the **smallest** zener current that occurs.
steps.explanation:
The load current is fixed: $I_L = {{VZ}}/{{RL}}$ = {{VZ/RL|A}}. $I_Z$ is smallest when $I_R$ is smallest, i.e. at minimum supply:
$I_{Z} = \frac{ {{Vmin}} - {{VZ}} }{ {{R}} } - {{VZ/RL}}$ = {{(Vmin-VZ)/R - VZ/RL|A}}.
(At maximum supply it would be {{(Vmax-VZ)/R - VZ/RL|A}}.)

steps.prompt: The graph shows the $i_D$–$v_D$ characteristic of a zener diode (usual diode references). Read its zener voltage $V_Z$ (as a positive number).
steps.explanation: A zener conducts in reverse when $v_D$ reaches $-V_Z$: the curve drops almost vertically at $v_D$ ≈ {{-VZ|V}}, so $V_Z$ ≈ {{VZ|V}}. Because the line is so steep, the voltage hardly changes over a wide range of current, which is what makes the zener a voltage reference. (The steep rise at about +0.7 V is ordinary forward conduction.)

steps.prompt: In breakdown a real zener behaves like a source $V_{Z0}$ in series with a small resistance $R_Z$. The graph shows the reverse current $I_Z$ versus the reverse voltage $v_Z$. Use the two marked points to find $R_Z$.
steps.explanation: Between the marked points the current rises from 20 mA to 40 mA while the voltage rises from {{VZ0+0.02*RZ|V}} to {{VZ0+0.04*RZ|V}}. $R_Z = \Delta v_Z/\Delta I_Z$ = {{0.02*RZ|V}} / 20 mA = {{RZ|Ω}}. The line meets $I_Z$ = 0 at $V_{Z0}$ = {{VZ0|V}}.

steps.prompt: A zener regulator ($V_Z$ = 5 V) feeds a load resistor. Which graph shows the output voltage $v_o$ while the supply $V_s$ is slowly raised from 0? ($V_s$ horizontal, $v_o$ vertical, same scales.)
steps.explanation: While the divider voltage $V_sR_L/(R+R_L)$ is below $V_Z$ the zener does not conduct, so $v_o$ rises in proportion to $V_s$. Once it reaches $V_Z$ the zener breaks down and holds $v_o$ at $V_Z$ = 5 V: the graph bends into a flat line. A line that keeps rising means no regulation; the output never sits at 5 V for small $V_s$ (there is no source of 5 V then) and it does not jump.

steps.prompt: For a zener shunt regulator with a load resistor, the graph shows $v_o$ versus the supply voltage $V_s$. Read the smallest supply voltage for which the output is regulated.
steps.explanation: Regulation starts at the knee, where the divider voltage $V_sR_L/(R+R_L)$ reaches $V_Z$ and the zener starts to conduct: $V_s$ ≈ {{Vsm|V}}. Here $R$ = {{R|Ω}} and $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}, so $V_{s,min} = V_Z(R+R_L)/R_L$ = {{VZ|V}} × {{(R+RL)/RL||3}} = {{Vsm|V}}. Below the knee the slope is $R_L/(R+R_L)$ = {{RL/(R+RL)||2}}.

steps.prompt: Curves A (green) and B (red) show $v_o$ versus $V_s$ for the same zener regulator with two different load resistors. Which curve belongs to the **smaller** load resistance (the heavier load)?
steps.explanation: Before breakdown the output is the divider voltage $V_sR_L/(R+R_L)$. A smaller $R_L$ gives a smaller fraction, so the rising part is **flatter** and a higher supply is needed before the zener takes over. The curve whose knee lies further to the right belongs to the heavier load.
